🇷🇺 ⚡️ 🇪🇺 Europe’s Gas Gamble Pays Off — For Russia EU buyers spent $13.5B on Russian gas in the first nine months of 2026, about 10% more than a year earlier in euro terms. By September, with the ban on Russian gas arriving by sea just three months away, the bloc’s monthly bill for Russian gas had reached $1.47B, about 50% more than a year earlier. Tankers accounted for the bigger share. EU buyers spent $7.80B on Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG), up nearly 12%, and $5.64B on gas delivered by pipeline, up 6%, according to Eurostat trade figures compiled by RIA Novosti. France still takes cargoes from Russia’s Yamal LNG project, where French energy company TotalEnergies holds a stake. Hungary still receives Russian gas through the TurkStream pipeline. Europe also had less gas in reserve when it needed it most. The disruption to Qatari exports pushed up the cost of filling underground storage over the summer. Buyers who held out for cheaper gas went into the heating season with less time to buy it. By mid-November, EU storage was around 70% full. Those reserves usually let utilities ride out a cold spell without having to pay whatever a seller asks that week. With less gas in storage and much of Qatar’s supply still off the market, European buyers have to compete with Asian importers for tankers that can still change destination. On January 1, 2027, the EU ban reaches the long-term contracts that still allow Russian LNG into European ports. Russian pipeline gas faces a September 30 cutoff. The European Commission can give an individual country until November 1 if it determines that the country risks missing its storage target. For European industry, the price of securing replacement gas matters even if every cargo arrives on time. A fertilizer plant needs natural gas to make ammonia. A glassmaker needs it to fire its furnaces. Both have to sell against producers that can buy the same fuel for less. Europe can bid high enough to keep the gas flowing this winter. Its factories have less room to maneuver.
